Before you read your results
Your Crown lease
In the ACT, residential land is held under a Crown lease, not freehold title. Your lease has a purpose clause that says what can be built on the block. Many leases in Canberra are limited to a single dwelling. If yours is, that restriction applies regardless of what the planning rules permit - a lease variation through a development application is required before a second dwelling can be built or sold separately, and a Lease Variation Charge (LVC) applies. Depending on your suburb, this can range from around $46,000 to well over $300,000.
If you are in RZ1 and considering dual occupancy, check whether you qualify for the [ LINK: ACT Government's RZ1 LVC Partial Waiver  revenue.act.gov.au/rates-and-property-charges/lease-variation-charge-lvc/rz1-lease-variation-charge-lvc-partial-waiver ]

BlockPlanner is actively engaging with the ACT Government to push for fairer LVC treatment for resident-led projects. If the LVC would affect the feasibility of your project, we would like to hear from you.
[LINK: Share your experience with the LVC - takes 2 minutes]

Your easements
Your title may also have easements - legal rights held by third parties over part of your land. You cannot build over an easement, and depending where one sits it can significantly affect what is practical in the rear yard. The easement data in this report comes from ACTmapi deposited plans and is indicative only - not all easements registered on title will appear here. A title search confirms what actually applies.

A granny flat is the most common example - a self-contained home on the same block as your existing house with its own entrance, kitchen, bathroom, and living space. YES copy:
Under the Territory Plan, dual occupancy housing means "the use of land that was originally used or leased for the purposes of single dwelling housing for two dwellings." It is a form of multi-unit housing. Both homes can be lived in, rented, or sold as a package. To sell them separately you need to take an extra step - unit titling, covered below.

Your block qualifies.

All buildings on the block combined cannot cover more than 45% of the total block area. That includes the existing house, the new dwelling, garage, and any other roofed structures. Whether a second dwelling fits comfortably alongside what is already there depends on house position, rear yard depth, and what the 45% coverage limit and setback requirements leave to work with.

Building a second dwelling and pursuing unit titling both require a development application (DA). The DA covers construction approval. Unit titling also requires a lease variation as part of that process. Check your Crown lease before committing to anything.

YES copy:
Under the Territory Plan, dual occupancy housing means "the use of land that was originally used or leased for the purposes of single dwelling housing for two dwellings." It is a form of multi-unit housing. Both homes can be lived in, rented, or sold as a package. To sell them separately, see unit titling below.

Your block qualifies.

RZ2 allows more dwellings on larger blocks. The formula is one additional dwelling per 250m² or part thereof over the 700m² minimum. A 950m² block is 250m² over the minimum, giving at least two dwellings total. Site coverage across all buildings cannot exceed 45% of the block area. If street frontage is under 20m, the maximum is three dwellings regardless of block size.

If your block is between 600 and 699m², a second pathway exists where all dwellings must be built to the AS4299 Class C accessible design standard - wider doorways, step-free entry, accessible bathrooms throughout. That is a real design and cost commitment.

Building a second dwelling and pursuing unit titling both require a development application (DA). Check your Crown lease before committing to anything.

YES copy:
Unit titling is the process that gives each dwelling on a dual occupancy its own separate title, making each independently sellable. It is the step that turns a construction project into two distinct assets.

Your block qualifies.

Both dwellings must be built and have a Certificate for Occupancy and Use before the unit title can be registered. You cannot sell bare land in RZ1 - construction comes first. One of the two dwellings must also be 120m² or less in floor area, excluding the garage. This is a condition of unit titling specifically, not a general design rule - the other dwelling can be larger.

What the process involves: constructing the dwellings requires a development application (DA). The unit titling itself also requires a lease variation as part of that DA process. Together this constitutes a significant development application. Check your Crown lease before committing to a design direction.

The ACT Government currently offers a stamp duty exemption on the first sale of a unit titled RZ1 property. Confirm current eligibility and expiry with the ACT Revenue Office before factoring this into any numbers.

There is more to the picture.

The options above are based on your block size and zone. They tell you what the planning rules permit in principle. What actually works on your specific block depends on what is already there.

Trees. Significant trees are protected under the Urban Forest Act 2023. A protected tree has a Tree Protection Zone - an area around the trunk and canopy where you cannot build or excavate without approval. Depending where trees sit, they can reduce usable space or rule out certain configurations entirely. This assessment flags significant trees based on canopy size from aerial imagery. We also separately check the ACTmapi Registered Trees layer - individually listed trees with a higher level of protection.

Easements. Depending on where an easement sits on your block, it can significantly affect where a second dwelling can go. The paid report maps what's visible from ACTmapi for your specific block.

Heritage. If the property is within a heritage overlay, development proposals need to respond to heritage requirements. Our assessment uses the ACTmapi heritage layer. If heritage applies, free preliminary advice is available through the ACT Government's heritage architecture service: [PLACEHOLDER - Philip Leasing Architects link].

Sewer. Where the sewer connection sits affects where a second dwelling can be serviced and what it costs.

District policies. Additional planning requirements may apply on top of zone rules depending on your suburb - particularly in the Inner North and City districts.

Subdivision and Leasing Policy. For blocks where subdivision is being considered, NI2023-540 F01 (Subdivision Policy) and F02 (Leasing Policy) apply in addition to the zone rules. A registered town planner can advise on what this means for a specific proposal.
